Unit 14 (Chemistry in Everyday Life) is sourced from the chemistry half of "FAST TRACK IPE for Sr. Students", book pp.105-106, printed chapter "11. CHEMISTRY IN EVERYDAY LIFE"; the book prints this question on book p.105 as VSAQ 8. Neither the two-book union check nor a board back-test was possible for Chemistry-II: the TSBIE Basic Learning Material on hand is physics-only and first-year, and no second-year chemistry paper is in the corpus. BOOK ERROR (book p.105, VSAQ 7 and VSAQ 8): the printed definitions of antiseptic and disinfectant are the same sentence with the words rearranged, and neither says where the chemical is applied. The distinction is added here: a disinfectant is applied on a non-living surface, an antiseptic on living tissue. BOOK GAP: the book prints "1% Phenol solution" without saying that 0.2% phenol is an antiseptic, so the one example that shows a compound changing class with concentration is lost. It is written on this card and on ts_ipe_c2_cel_antiseptics, and the two cards are written to agree. BOOK OMISSION: formalin is given as an example with no statement of what it is; it is about a 40 per cent solution of formaldehyde in water, and that is stated here.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: The definition
lines: They are applied on non-living surfaces
such as floors, drains and instruments.
They are too harmful for living tissue.
steps.why: A disinfectant and an antiseptic do the same thing to a micro-organism, so the action alone cannot earn the mark. What separates them is the surface: a disinfectant is used on a non-living surface, and it is too harmful to be put on skin.
common_mistakes: Writing the definition without saying where it is applied. That same sentence also defines an antiseptic.
Writing that a disinfectant can be applied on a wound. It is too harmful for living tissue.
steps.memory_tip: Disinfectant goes on a floor or a drain; antiseptic goes on skin.
steps.margin_note: The words non-living surface are the whole mark. Without them this reads as an antiseptic answer.

steps.label: Examples and the concentration boundary
lines: Formalin is about a 40% solution of
Chlorine at 0.2 to 0.4 ppm in water and
sulphur dioxide in low concentration are
steps.why: The concentration is part of the example here, not decoration. Phenol at 0.2 per cent is dilute enough to be used on skin as an antiseptic; at 1 per cent it is used only on a non-living surface. Chlorine at a few tenths of a part per million is the amount used to disinfect drinking water.
common_mistakes: Writing phenol as a disinfectant with no concentration. The concentration is what makes the statement true.
Giving dettol or tincture of iodine as disinfectants. Both are antiseptics, applied on living tissue.
steps.memory_tip: Phenol at 1 per cent is a disinfectant; at 0.2 per cent it is an antiseptic.
steps.margin_note: Two examples finish this mark. The phenol line also shows that the definition above is the right one.

insider_note: The mark depends on the boundary with antiseptics. Write where the chemical is applied, a non-living surface here, and give the 0.2% and 1% phenol pair; that one line separates the two classes.
